item.title: The Big Divide in Approaches to Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

The Big Divide in Approaches to Therapy

When therapists stop being the expert.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists can help clients access their inner wisdom rather than acting as the expert.
  • Focusing on clients' internal experiences enables deeper self-understanding and meaningful change.
  • The real divide in therapy is between being told how to change and discovering change through self-awareness.
Source: Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash

For many years, I operated under the assumption that, as a therapist, I was supposed to be the expert in the room. I thought my role was to lead the charge, offer insightful observations, and provide suggestions about how clients should approach their lives and relationships.

But around COVID, I discovered therapeutic approaches that challenged that assumption. In Hakomi and Internal Family Systems (IFS)-informed therapy, there is an emphasis on helping clients access their own inner wisdom rather than relying solely on the therapist’s interpretations and advice.

My role began to feel more like that of a midwife, helping clients bring forth and integrate what is already within them. The idea is to create the conditions in which qualities such as calm, clarity, compassion, and self-understanding can become more accessible. This means allowing clients to lead the way, sometimes described as “riding the tail of the comet.”

Ironically, this is much harder than it sounds. It requires me to let go of my interpretations, advice, and even my well-intentioned agendas. Instead, I am learning to lean into the ambiguity that comes with each client and trust the process rather than rush toward an answer.

Some therapists describe themselves as being very direct with clients. They may use “tough love” to point out what they believe clients are doing wrong and encourage them to make different choices. This approach can be well-intentioned and sometimes helpful.

However, I have come to question whether being direct always leads to meaningful change. Sometimes, it can become another attempt to break through a client's denial without fully understanding what might be driving their behavior.

With my current approach, I am less interested in telling clients what is wrong with them and more interested in helping them understand why they may be stuck. Rather than viewing someone as bad, lazy, narcissistic, or incapable of recognizing the consequences of their actions, I consider whether some part of them is trying to protect them or make sense of their experiences.

This doesn't mean avoiding accountability. It means understanding the internal conflicts that can make change so difficult. This approach isn't simply about sitting back and listening while clients talk. In fact, I often invite clients to pay less attention to the stories they are telling and more attention to what happens inside them as they speak.

article continues after advertisement

I might ask them to pause, slow down, and notice what emerges. Perhaps they feel tension in their chest, an impulse to withdraw, an uncomfortable emotion, a memory, or a familiar belief about themselves. These experiences can offer clues about what is happening beneath the surface.

Rather than immediately interpreting what I observe, I invite clients to become curious about their own internal experiences. As they discover something, we explore it together and see what else might emerge. In this way, clients become active participants in their own self-discovery.

For people accustomed to traditional talk therapy, this can feel unfamiliar. It may be particularly uncomfortable for those who intellectualize, analyze, gather information, and try to make sense of everything cognitively. They may be accustomed to explaining their experiences without necessarily slowing down enough to feel them.

For some, this may be the first time they have had a space where they can simply pause and listen to what is happening inside them. One difference I appreciate about this way of working is the opportunity for clients to experience shifts during a session, rather than leaving with only another explanation of why they feel the way they do.

I know the value of this approach not only as a therapist but also as a therapy client. In my own life, I have become more aware of my reactivity, particularly my tendency to blame my wife when I feel hurt or defensive. Instead of automatically concluding that she has made me angry, I am learning to slow down and recognize the vulnerabilities underneath my reactions.

Sometimes, her words activate feelings that have less to do with the present moment and more to do with my own past experiences. When I can acknowledge those feelings, I have less need to respond defensively or strike back with hurtful words.

This doesn't mean that other people's behavior never contributes to our distress. Relationships involve real conflicts, and sometimes other people do need to take responsibility for their actions. But there is a difference between recognizing what someone else has done and assuming that our emotional reactions are entirely their responsibility to resolve.

article continues after advertisement

Whenever I feel activated, I am learning to ask myself a different question: “What is happening inside me right now?” Instead of immediately looking outward for someone to make me feel better, I can begin to understand what has been stirred up within me and what I might need to address. Sometimes, what I discover is a vulnerability that needs attention rather than an argument that needs to be won.

Perhaps the biggest divide isn't between different schools of therapy. It's between being told what we need to change and developing the awareness to discover it for ourselves. When we slow down enough to listen inwardly, we may begin to see our familiar patterns differently. And from that place of greater understanding, change becomes something we can participate in rather than something someone else tells us we need to do.

item.title: Reflected Glory and the Guillermo Rodriguez Phenomenon
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Reflected Glory and the Guillermo Rodriguez Phenomenon

The psychological phenomenon of “BIRG” provides an answer.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Fans can “bask in the reflected glory” of their favorite celebrity or team’s success, known as ‘BIRG.'
  • BIRG brings a sense of vicarious success that results in higher self esteem and positive sense of self.
  • The flip side of BIRG is CORF, cutting off reflected failure by distancing oneself when a favorite loses.
  • Both BIRG and CORF are forms of impression management fans use to create a positive public image.
Source: Juvo Des/Pixabay

Deadline recently ran the headline “Guillermo Rodriguez is finally getting his moment”. The Jimmy Kimmel sidekick, dancing with pro partner Witney Carson, has been the unexpected hit of the current season of Dancing With The Stars. Why all of a sudden are so many people Guillermo fans? A psychological phenomenon called ‘BIRG’ may be part of the answer.

The Appeal of the Underdog

Rodriguez’ appeal is not new – he became a “celebrity” when he went from quirky security guard to quirky onstage sidekick for Jimmy Kimmel, so he already had a fan base. Fans have appreciated his ability not to take himself too seriously and to “be himself”. Guillermo seems real at a time when we are all struggling to figure out what’s not real on a daily basis, making authenticity important.

He is also willing to be vulnerable in admitting when he’s not that good at something. The comments on the Deadline article included appreciation for his lack of pretense, one stating “The world needs more Guillermos and especially now!” Guillermo’s initial success in spite of an admitted lack of dancing prowess may have only made him more appealing to many fans. (He pulled open his shirt after one dance to reveal “Dancing 4 The People” written on his chest as an acknowledgement that it’s the fans’ passion and not his dancing skills that are responsible.) At a time when many people are feeling like it’s harder and harder to succeed in an increasingly stressful world, watching the underdog persevere and make it to the next episode has inspired many viewers.

Success Feels Good, Even When It’s Not Ours

Still, Rodriguez’ continuing success was unexpected, since the other dancers are more skilled. What explains the outpouring of support that’s keeping him on the show?

One explanation is simply that he IS successful, leading to others hoping to vicariously experience that success. There’s a psychological phenomenon that explains that called “Basking in reflected glory” or “BIRG”. BIRG is a term coined by social psychologist Robert Cialdini in the 70s to describe that feeling fans experience when their favorite wins – a rush of emotion that feels like they have won too even when they played no part at all in that success.

Cialdini found that proclaiming yourself a fan of someone who’s on a winning streak, like Guillermo is right now, enhances the fan’s positive image and self esteem. BIRG is a form of impression management, something we all do to show off our best qualities and create a positive public image, in this case by emphasizing a connection to a successful person.

Source: Lynn Zubernis

The BIRG phenomenon is responsible for the proliferation of everything from tee shirts to bumper stickers to celebrity-inspired hair styles that announce that someone is a fan of a celebrity or team that’s having a moment. When that person or team is winning, everyone wants to be their fan. In fact, so many fans are “basking in the reflected glory” of Guillermo’s initial success that they have continued voting in large enough numbers to keep him in the competition. Even the show’s judges seem to be BIRGing. “Just like everybody else,” judge Derek Hough said, “I’m obsessed with you.” Bruno Tonioli added, “I understand why you’re becoming a national obsession.”

The show’s official Instagram posted “We couldn’t be more obsessed with Guillermo and Witney’s Samba” after the most recent episode aired. In spite of very low scores from the judges (a 13 out of 30 for that Samba), so many fans voted for Rodriguez and Carson that they will be returning once again.

The Flip Side of BIRG

Of course, the opposite is also true. Identifying so strongly with a celebrity or band or sports team that you experience a vicarious sense of success when they are “winning” means that when they are not winning, that can be painful. Research shows that fans try to distance themselves from those failures by “cutting off reflected failure” or “CORFing”. In other words, it’s “we won” but “they lost”. As difficult as that might be for a celebrity to swallow, for fans that strategy protects their self esteem and positive self image.

It also means that wanting to avoid those painful feelings leaves fans highly motivated to keep their favorites winning – and to sometimes attack anyone who might be perceived as a threat to that success. Other DWTS contestants have their own fans, and some of those fans worry that their favorites will be sent home so Guillermo can stay. There have been accusations of the show being rigged to try to prevent that outcome, with viewers posting on the show’s Instagram that “He needs to go home, that is not dancing!!!”

But Guillermo fans show no signs of giving up, voting in large numbers to keep his success – and their basking in his reflected glory – going a while longer. All the way to the mirror ball? I guess we’ll see just how compelling BIRG can be!

item.title: Why Boomer Parents and Millennial Daughters Miscommunicate
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Why Boomer Parents and Millennial Daughters Miscommunicate

How everyday comments create emotional labor and distance between generations.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Parents and adult daughters often hold different expectations about loving and respectful communication.
  • A comment meant as a joke can threaten a daughter's sense of herself as a caring family member.
  • Daughters often take responsibility for repairing tension, even when they didn't create it.
  • Communication skills between daughters and parents can improve with effort and intentionality.

You finally have twenty free minutes, so you call your mom. She picks up and says, "Oh, hey, Miss Busy Lady! You've got so much going on that I feel like I barely get time with you."

She probably means it warmly, as playful affection with a little wistfulness mixed in. But the call you made to share good news has turned into something else. Now you're explaining your schedule, apologizing for being hard to reach, and reassuring her that she matters.

You reached out to connect. Yet somehow, you're now in the midst of repairing a disconnection you never meant to create. One exchange like this is nothing. Hundreds of them can make a relationship you value start to feel like sandpaper.

Millenials and Boomers in family conversations
Source: Claude

Two Ideas of What Love Sounds Like

Communication researchers Ascan Koerner and Mary Anne Fitzpatrick (2002) describe families along two dimensions. Families high in conformity orientation emphasize agreement, shared values, and hierarchy. Families high in conversation orientation encourage open discussion and the expression of different views.

These orientations show up in the words families use. In a study analyzing thousands of speech acts from real family conversations, Koerner and Kelly Cvancara (2002) found that families higher in conformity used relatively more advice, interpretation, and questions. Families lower in conformity used relatively more acknowledgment, reflection, and confirmation.

An important caveat: the researcher's theory describes a family's shared communication climate, not a generation's. There's no evidence that Boomer households, or Gen X households, were uniformly high in conformity. But the theory offers a useful lens for a common friction — a relational tension that shows up again and again. A parent may expect deference, reassurance, and automatic closeness. Her adult daughter may expect autonomy and mutual consideration.

Neither is wrong about what it means to love. They may simply disagree about what loving, respectful communication sounds like.

Why a Joke Can Sting

Sociologist Erving Goffman (1967) used the term face for the positive identity we claim in social interaction. Politeness researchers Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1987) later described "face-threatening acts": remarks that put that identity at risk, often without the speaker noticing.

article continues after advertisement

An adult daughter wants to be seen as loving, responsible, and competent. Then she invites her mother to dinner and hears, "Oh, you're inviting me? I didn't know I was important enough to be included, haha."

The "haha" signals a joke. The content signals a complaint: you haven't been a good enough daughter. Whomp whomp. Before she can enjoy the invitation she extended, she has to defend her standing as someone who cares. She’s feeling deflated right when she was trying to do good daughtering.

If she says the comment hurt, the parent might reply: "Everyone is so sensitive these days. You know I didn't mean it like that." That response asks the adult daughter to set aside her experience in favor of her parent's intention.

Humor isn't the problem. Teasing can be a real sign of closeness. The trouble starts when humor repeatedly carries criticism or disappointment in a form that's hard to address directly. Intention matters, but it doesn't fully determine impact.

The Invisible Work of Keeping the Peace

My research focuses on what happens after comments like these. In interviews with adult daughters ages 25 to 44, each with a healthy, living mother, I found that being a daughter is an active performance (Alford, 2021). It's ongoing work, often done out of lifelong habit, that I call daughtering.

A more recent study my colleagues and I conducted with daughters in difficult mother relationships found something striking (Alonso-Pecora et al., 2026). Even when daughters attributed problems to their mothers, many still took responsibility for managing the relationship.

The same pattern shows up in ordinary, loving relationships, just in smaller doses. A single phone call can involve all four kinds of daughtering work identified in my book, Good Daughtering (Alford, 2026):

  • Acting: calling, inviting, explaining, apologizing, and following up.
  • Thinking: predicting how a parent will interpret her words.
  • Feeling: managing her own frustration while tending to her parent's disappointment.
  • Being: enacting what it means to be a good daughter and good person.

Family researchers have long observed that women tend to do the "kinkeeping" that holds families together. A daughter smoothing over a teasing remark is kinkeeping in real time. When she absorbs the responsibility for keeping every interaction pleasant, connection starts to feel like a chore.

article continues after advertisement

Three Small Changes That Create More Connection

If you're a daughter, this is a section you might share with your parent. If you're a parent, this is where small shifts make the biggest difference.

Instead of saying: "Oh, hey, Miss Busy Pants! You've got so much going on that I feel like I barely get time with you, haha." Try saying: "I'm so happy to hear from you! What’s going on in your life?”

Instead of saying: "Everyone is so sensitive these days. You know I didn't mean it like that." Try saying: "I didn't mean for it to land like that. Let me try that again."

Instead of saying: "Oh, you're inviting me? I didn't know I was important enough to be included, haha." Try saying: "I'd love to come! Thanks for thinking of me."

Three principles sit underneath these replacements:

  1. Express affection without suggesting guilt. A request for connection is easier to answer when it doesn't also demand reassurance.
  2. Respond to impact, not just intention. Acknowledging someone's experience doesn't require abandoning your own perspective.
  3. Reward reaching out. When a daughter calls or invites, respond to the invitation before raising disappointment about the past.

The same words can land very differently depending on the relationship around them. A 2021 daily-diary study of young adults found that those with more strained parent relationships were more likely to experience parental advice as unwanted, and unwanted advice was linked to worse mood (Wang et al., 2021). Small, consistent changes in how affection is expressed help build the kind of relationship where comments are heard generously.

Connection Shouldn't Be One Person's Job

Parents don't have to stop joking or feeling disappointed, or even stop wanting more time with their daughters. But they can learn to say those things more directly, with more room for their daughters' autonomy. And, meanwhile, daughters can recognize that feeling drained by these exchanges doesn't mean they love their parents any less. Lots of true things can coexist.

article continues after advertisement

The goal isn't for parents and daughters to say everything perfectly. It's to create relationships where both people can show up as themselves, without one person having to do all the emotional work of keeping them connected.

item.title: What Women Say They Want From Men May Surprise You
item.description:
Relationships

What Women Say They Want From Men May Surprise You

What women valued most wasn't status. It was connection.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional support matters more than material provision.
  • Respect is the most foundational relationship need.
  • Trust and communication are key cornerstones as well.
  • Women are seeking partners, not perfect profiles.

“Listen.” It was only one word, but it represents one of the most striking themes that emerged in my survey of women who were asked what they need most from the men in their lives. Women focused not on status, grand gestures, or wealth but on characteristics that run deeper than these things. They want partners who are emotionally available, respectful, trustworthy, and willing to communicate openly.

These insights came from my online survey that grew out of a 2018 Psychology Today post exploring what women want from men in romantic relationships. Between 2018 and 2023, 108 women completed the survey, sharing their perspectives on the qualities they value most in a partner. Although the respondents do not represent a scientific sample of all women, their responses offer a revealing glimpse into the characteristics many associate with healthy, satisfying relationships.

We all know that a charming smile, an adorable dog, and a well-placed bestselling book can make for an appealing dating profile. But while those things may capture someone's attention, they’re unlikely to build a lasting connection. Women in this survey were far more likely to talk about trust, respect, emotional support, and partnership than profile-perfect accessories. The consistency of these responses suggests that many qualities women value most have less to do with impressing them and more to do with understanding them.

Listening to the Data

In reviewing responses from women about what they most need from men, I was struck by the consistency of their answers. While women are certainly not a monolith, the themes that surfaced overwhelmingly touched on emotionally healthy relationships characterized by respect, trust, support, communication, and genuine partnership.

Women Want Emotional Support

“Understanding and empathetic listening without trying to fix things”

One of the strongest themes reflected a desire for emotional connection and support. Women repeatedly described wanting partners who are understanding, compassionate, empathetic, and emotionally available. They wanted someone who would listen, offer comfort during challenging times, and provide reassurance when life becomes challenging.

Interestingly, many respondents did not simply ask for love. They asked to be understood. There is an important distinction between those two things. Love can be spoken; understanding must be demonstrated. Feeling understood creates emotional safety, and emotional safety is often the foundation upon which intimacy and trust are built.

Women Want Respect

“To feel heard and respected”

If there was one word that appeared again and again throughout the responses, it was respect. Women described wanting to be respected for who they are, for their choices, their opinions, their goals, and their individuality. They wanted to be treated as equals rather than as people whose role is simply to support someone else's needs.

Women Want Trust and Honesty

"Women most need loyalty, honesty, and accountability."

Trust was another recurring theme. Women frequently identified honesty, loyalty, accountability, and integrity as essential relationship qualities. They wanted partners whose words and actions aligned and whose behavior created confidence rather than uncertainty.

Women Want Communication

"The ability to talk freely about feelings both good and bad and to be heard"

Communication was also mentioned repeatedly. Many respondents specifically referenced listening, open dialogue, honest conversations, and the ability to discuss feelings. They wanted partners who could communicate clearly and who were willing to engage in meaningful conversations rather than avoid them.

Women Want Love, Affection, and Intimacy

“Love and affection and acceptance”

Women frequently described a desire for both emotional and physical expressions of love. Affection, romance, intimacy, and feeling cherished were mentioned as experiences that help relationships stay emotionally close and satisfying over time.

Women Want Safety

“We need to feel safe in our own homes”

Another frequently mentioned theme was safety. This included physical safety, emotional safety, stability, consistency, and security within the relationship. Women need partners who offer a sense of safety and support.

Women Want Partnership

“To work together as a team”

A particularly strong theme was the desire for true, egalitarian partnerships. Relationships aren’t easy, and women want a partner who shares responsibilities, decision-making, and emotional labor. They don’t simply want someone who can provide; they want someone who will participate. They want a true partner who contributes emotionally to the relationship, supports their goals, and helps carry the practical work of everyday life.

Women Want Friendship

“Acceptance, support, friendship, love”

Many respondents shared their desire for a partner who is also a friend. Beyond romance, they valued companionship, one of the foundations of lasting relationships. They want someone with whom they can share their day-to-day lives and the bigger challenges in life. Friendship may sound like a tame ask of a partner, but genuine friendship is the glue that holds relationships together over the decades.

Women Want Authenticity

“An opportunity to be ourselves (participate in activities we enjoy, try those things we’ve always wanted to try) without being judged or held back because of a preconceived idea of what we should be doing.”

Women expressed the desire to feel accepted for who they are, not pressured to become someone else. They valued relationships in which they felt free to pursue their own interests, speak their minds, and grow as individuals without criticism or judgment. Authenticity allows partners to flourish when they are safe enough to be their true selves in the relationship.

Although the themes emerged separately, they point toward the same underlying need: Women want relationships in which they can feel safe, supported, valued, and fully themselves.

What Women Rarely Mentioned

Very few women emphasized wealth, status, prestige, social influence, or physical attractiveness as their primary needs in a relationship. Those may be nice to have, but they are not going to be enough on their own. Relationships take work, and if someone doesn’t seem ready or willing to share the labor, the “nice-to-have’s” won’t suffice.

The Bigger Takeaway

Perhaps the most revealing finding was not what women said, but what they rarely mentioned. Wealth, prestige, status, and physical appearance appeared only occasionally. Instead, women consistently described wanting partners who can be emotionally present, trustworthy, respectful, supportive, and willing to share life's burdens and joys. They want partners in the full sense of the word.

While women are certainly not a monolith, these responses point to a surprisingly simple truth: women are not looking for perfection. They're looking for connection, respect, and partnership. And those may be the very qualities that sustain healthy relationships for everyone.

item.title: Why Mass Hysteria Still Explains ‘Havana Syndrome’
item.description:
Intelligence

Why Mass Hysteria Still Explains ‘Havana Syndrome’

A response to Dr. Eric Haseltine’s critique of the psychogenic model

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • There remains no clear evidence to that the symptoms are the result of an attack by a covert weapon.
  • While 'Havana Syndrome' remains contentious, a psychological origin is still the most likely explanation.
  • Dr Eric Haseltine's thoughtful review should be tempered with the evidence against a directed energy attack.

Dr Eric Haseltine, a former American intelligence officer and neuroscientist, has expressed skepticis in his Psychology Today blog (Long Fuse, Big Bang), that “mass hysteria… does not explain much of the data from studies of victims, and remains an unproven hypothesis.” ‘Havana Syndrome’ refers to an array of health complaints first reported by U.S. diplomats and intelligence officers stationed in Havana, Cuba in 2015. Technically, it does not fit the definition of a syndrome since the symptoms and course were so variable, but to avoid confusion, we have placed quotation marks around the term.

What we argued

Dr. Haseltine's column is more measured than most criticisms of the psychogenic explanation, which we appreciate, but several of his objections rest on a version of our argument that we never made, and others are answered in our book he cites [1].

Neurologist Robert Baloh and I have never claimed that all or even most of the reports of Anomalous Health Incident (AHIs) share a single cause, or that those affected are malingering (feigning illness). Psychogenic illness can affect anyone, and the symptoms are real. The conclusions of the two “prestigious expert panels” that Dr. Haseltine cites as suggesting microwave radiation as a likely cause, were both chaired by the same person and their findings were rejected in 2023 and 2025 by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence [2, 3]. The intelligence community consensus judged it “highly unlikely” that a foreign adversary was responsible, and that the symptoms were probably the result of preexisting conditions, conventional illnesses and environmental factors.

The two panels cited by Dr. Haseltine were flawed. The National Academy of Sciences panel stated that there was no epidemiological evidence on the social patterning of cases, making it impossible to adequately assess psychogenic illness as an explanation [4]. However, they failed to acknowledge an investigation which detailed the early social patterning starting with ‘patient zero.’ This information was first published in February 2018 by two Pulitzer Prize-winning journalists who travelled to Cuba and conducted over three dozen interviews [5, 6]. The second panel cited by Dr. Haseltine, dismissed the psychogenic explanation on the erroneous grounds that intelligence officers and diplomats were not prone to experiencing psychogenic illness due to their training [7].

Dr. Haseltine writes that “Several medical studies reported objective clinical findings, including vestibular and oculomotor abnormalities.” This is misleading. The most serious symptoms were brain damage, white matter tract changes, and hearing loss, and while widely reported in the media, they were never demonstrated. For instance, a 2019 study in the Journal of the American Medical Association identified brain anomalies in the U.S. diplomats in Cuba [8]. Media outlets jumped on this story and it was widely reported that the victims were suffering from “brain damage.” But in the ‘Discussion’ section of the study, the authors admitted that the anomalies were relatively minor and could have been caused by individual variation. Also absent from most news reports was the observation that it is not uncommon to find minor brain anomalies in small cohorts that are under long-term stress. Brain anomalies are not the equivalent of brain damage. Another often overlooked factor has been the use of advanced brain imaging that is notoriously difficult to interpret as it produces a massive number of data points that unlike regular MRIs, are so complex they can only be understood with sophisticated computer programs and generate false positives as high as 70 percent [1]. As for the claims of hearing loss in some victims, that was a result of media reports that turned out to be untrue [1].

A More Plausible Explanation

When you remove claims of brain damage and hearing loss, you are left with a long list of symptoms. These include headaches, dizziness, nausea, forgetfulness, confusion, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, balance problems, tinnitus, ear pain, head pressure, insomnia, and depression. These symptoms are common in any population. A 2014 study surveyed 1,000 people who were read a list 46 symptoms and asked if they had experienced any over the previous seven days. The average was five. Over 30 percent reported fatigue and headaches while about 30 percent said they had insomnia. Over 10 percent reported difficulty concentrating, depressed mood, memory problems, eye or vision issues, and ear or hearing problems. Nausea and dizziness came in at about 8 percent [9]. These are symptoms of ‘Havana Syndrome’

A mechanism is not an exposure

Haseltine's simulation suggests pulsed Radio Frequency waves could, in principle, injure tissue, and he candidly says it does not prove that it did. But a plausible model is not evidence that anyone was exposed. The ‘Havana Syndrome’ attack explanation requires energy delivered through walls into bedrooms and hotel rooms, to chosen individuals, unnoticed by the person in the next bed, and without burns. Ric Tell, who spent decades on exposure standards, noted that damaging brain tissue would mean heating it to the point of cooking [1]. Sharon Weinberger’s review in Nature found that fifty years of research had produced no usable microwave weapon [1]. After a decade, nobody has produced a device, a signal, or a measurement of energy at any site. A major problem with the public understanding ‘Havana Syndrome’ is that it has been politicized. A 2024 Congressional hearing was presumptuously titled: “Silent Weapons: Examining Foreign Anomalous Health Incidents Targeting Americans in the Homeland and Abroad.” [10]

The timeline and symptom pattern

Dr. Haseltine asks how contagion can explain people who fell ill alone at night before they knew of other cases. Embassy personnel that we talked to were adamant that this was not the case: everyone knew [1]. A former CIA officer described that first patient as aggressively lobbying people to connect their health complaints to the sounds [11]. He even played his recording at an embassy gathering, urging them to report their symptoms [12]. His recording was later identified to be that of the Indies short-tailed cricket [13]. The reports that emerged after the story was created, are what we would expect if the story shaped how people remembered ordinary sensations. Haseltine’s own The Spy in Moscow Station shows that the narrative was part of intelligence lore long before 2015. That is an ingredient for a nocebo response, not an objection to one. If the story is a sound that strikes you at home, expect reports of sound, pressure and directionality. And then there are the crickets. A loud insect calling nearby would seem to start and stop as a person moves about, which is the very pattern he offers as evidence against a psychogenic explanation.

The medical findings

The Penn study used healthy volunteers as controls. Twelve patients had previous concussions and none of the controls did, and the imaging relied on complex computer processing with high false-positives [1]. Almost any symptomatic group would differ from healthy controls. The most rigorous work came after our book. In 2024, National Institute of Health researchers found no significant evidence of MRI-detectable brain injury, and no differences in most clinical measures, among subjects who experienced these incidents compared with controls. Saying that later studies “did not find differences on all measures” understates that result [14, 15].

Who is being victimized?

Dr. Haseltine worries that calling these illnesses psychogenic will wound people twice. But the opposite is also true as fear sustains symptoms. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof. A decade has now passed without a weapon or clear evidence of exposure. Maybe someday evidence will be produced to prove that American diplomats and spies are being zapped by energy weapons, but right now there remains no credible evidence to suggest that this has happened.

item.title: What People Get Wrong About Skepticism
item.description:
Bias

What People Get Wrong About Skepticism

Skepticism isn't about being cynical or close-minded.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Skepticism isn't license to promote personal beliefs without evidence or research.
  • Critical thinkers accept "no decision" if evidence is insufficient, avoiding rushed conclusions.

Last week, I got some useful feedback on a post from earlier this year, Why “Do Your Own Research” Is Bad Advice. The feedback, from a friend who also teaches critical thinking, focused on one line that stood out: Don’t confuse skepticism with justification to promote your own opinion. Of course, I meant: If you are skeptical of a point of view, good; then investigate the research literature on that topic further. Don’t assume, because you’re skeptical of a concept, what you believe is correct by default.

The received feedback extended to an example of how people conflate skepticism with justification: the observation that many say things like, ‘I don't believe anything I hear on the news’ and, then, in the next breath, parrot off some spiel they learned from the one news source with which they do agree. I have observed many such arguments where once an individual has established that they are skeptical of an idea, it’s as if they feel they've finished all the heavy lifting with respect to good thinking and then, once established as skeptical, somehow have carte blanche to posit whatever they think to be true as fact. Sources be damned!

What, really, is skepticism? Skepticism refers to a process associated with: the challenging of ideas; withholding judgment before engaging all the evidence or when the evidence and reasons are insufficient; looking at findings from various perspectives; and the taking of a position and the ability to change position when the evidence and reasons are sufficient (Dwyer, 2017; 2025; Dwyer and colleagues, 2016). From a critical thinking perspective, skepticism refers to a disposition toward critical thinking; the latter being an inclination, tendency, or willingness to perform a given thinking skill (Dwyer, 2017; Facione, Facione and Giancarlo, 1997; Ku, 2009; Valenzuela, Nieto and Saiz, 2011).

How Critical Thinkers Approach Uncertainty and Decision-Making

Critical thinkers are often content to abstain from a decision when they know they need more information or time to process that information. They’re okay with ‘no decision’ for the time being. That’s because ‘no decision’ is typically better than the wrong decision. When we are skeptical, we can choose not to accept an idea because we might decide there is insufficient evidence available. But critical thinkers also know that the void left by that indecision does not have to be filled right away, as if by some place-marker for truth. Critical thinking requires objectively evaluating all possibilities; critical thinkers don't adopt an alternative conclusion by default. One idea doesn’t necessarily affect another. Both ideas can be wrong.

For example, some people get a hard time when involved in collaborative decision-making when, as part of their evaluation, they identify an issue with the proposed solution. For example, “I don’t think this solution will work because of x, y, and z.” A natural response may be: ‘Well, then you come up with something better!’ I understand why people would reply this way, but it remains that the onus isn’t really on the person who identified the issue to do this. By rights, they should be commended for identifying the issue with the solution before it was implemented. From a critical-thinking standpoint, they are right to halt the decision-making process, even if it means there is no decision for the time being. Of course, that only works if they have evidence on why it won’t work. Saying it won’t work without evidence is akin to cynicism.

article continues after advertisement

Perhaps a broader, useful analogy is war. When two groups are at war, it’s natural for those not directly involved to take sides; some level of bias will always creep into our judgment. However, just because you are against one side (because what they have done is ‘wrong’ or even criminal), they are labeled the bad guys, rightfully. It doesn’t mean that the other side is necessarily good by default. Both sides could well be ‘bad guys,’ and neither might deserve your support. Similarly, I've written about the U.S. party system here in similar ways. Just because you don’t like Democratic Party policies doesn’t make you a Republican and vice versa. Decision-making is not black and white. Sometimes, the only practical decision isn’t a good one, but rather the best bad decision or ‘lesser of evils.’ Other times, the best decision is no decision, until an acceptable one is developed.

The feedback got me thinking about what skepticism is and what it isn't. Consistent with the example in the feedback, skepticism is not being ‘skeptical’ of every idea thrown at you until you hear one that matches your existing worldview. No, that’s confirmation bias. This is not skepticism; a person may pretend to be skeptical to persuade their audience they are thinking critically, but that’s not the case. They are close-minded to all ideas inconsistent with their own.

Skepticism Is Not Cynicism

Many differences lie between them, but one is particularly relevant here. Skeptics, though not easily convinced, are open-minded to changing their perspective in light of sufficient evidence. Cynics likewise show scepticism, but when presented with sufficient evidence, they move the goalposts through illogical reasoning that makes the evidence insufficient to change perspective. Other times, they might dismiss an idea outright with irrelevant statements of distrust or bad faith; and we’ve all done this from time to time.

For example, when a billionaire starts a charity fund alongside a substantial donation for some worthy cause, many people might jump to the cynical conclusion that it’s just a PR stunt or a tax write-off. I imagine most people, like me, have made similar conclusions about similar examples, and that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re wrong. Maybe it is a PR opportunity. But the problem is, there’s no discernible way to progress good thinking from such a statement. Unless you were in that boardroom, you can’t possibly know the motivation. The critical thinker, on the other hand, might question the motive. They ask, what proportion of the donations reach the people who need it? Is this charity actually doing good? Is it funding nefarious activities? If it’s all positives, maybe we should support it, regardless of what we believe about motivations.

Skepticism is crucial for good thinking. But it’s not about being cynical or waiting around until you’re presented with an idea that you already believe. It’s being cautious about what you accept as true and being willing and open-minded to differing perspectives and sufficient evidence when presented.

item.title: Our Next Revolution in Medicine? The Bioelectronic Frontier
item.description:
Vagus Nerve

Our Next Revolution in Medicine? The Bioelectronic Frontier

Better regulation of the vagus nerve may reduce our need for medications.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Low grade inflammation is a feature of many of our common chronic conditions.
  • The vagus nerve plays an essential role in regulating inflammation.
  • Vagus nerve stimulation reduces inflammation.
  • Bioelectronic medicine has the potential to revolutionize our use of medications in chronic illnesses.

Drugs these days are both life-saving and lethal. A century ago, in this country, there were hardly any approved drugs for any illnesses, and drug abuse was rare. Now we have a drug for every ailment—more than we can count—and our epidemic of drug abuse puts panhandlers on the street corners of every city. Who would dispute that pharmacology has revolutionized the practice of medicine, as well as our culture? Without these marvelous medications, many of us middle-aged and elderly would be miserable or dead.

And yet I’m sure that future generations—hopefully the next one—will look back on many of our modern pharmacology treatments as crude, wasteful, risky, and unnecessarily expensive. Every pill we swallow and every IV solution infused works by saturating our whole body to reach one or a few intended target organs. Imagine how outraged we would be if, in order for one farmer to get his cotton fields treated for boll weevils, the whole state of Alabama had to be sprayed with insecticide. The “side effects,” both physical and political, would be intolerable to the people.

Political revolutions are sparked by crises. Scientific revolutions are sparked by inventions. Currently in the US, we have both an economic crisis—a health care system we can’t afford—and a period of underrecognized scientific invention.

Since revolutions are quieter in medicine than in politics, you may not be aware that the next revolution in medicine has already started. Kevin J. Tracey, MD, in The Great Nerve: The New Science of the Vagus Nerve and How to Harness Its Healing Reflexes (2025). writes: “We are in the early decades of a revolution in medicine, one that is launching previously unimaginable computerized electronic therapies to treat dangerous and disabling illnesses.” In declaring “bioelectronic medicine” as the next frontier, Tracey focuses on the role of the vagus nerve in inflammation and presents the evidence that vagus nerve stimulation can heal disorders of inflammation more effectively with less cost and less risk than our current medications for these disorders.

If inflammation seems too narrow a target for medicine’s next revolution, consider the range of common chronic conditions in which inflammation plays a primary or a secondary role: diabetes, coronary heart disease, obesity, arthritis, chronic pain syndromes, fibromyalgia, depression, Crohn’s Disease, ulcerative colitis, all autoimmune disorders, and many cancers, especially in their advanced stages.

Back in 2002, Tracey published a ground-breaking review titled “The Inflammatory Reflex” in which he spelled out how the vagus nerve—the two branches of which reach from our brainstem to every organ in our body—regulates the immune system. Since then, as a neurosurgeon, president and CEO of The Feinstein Institutes, and professor at the Zucker School of Medicine on Long Island, Tracey has focused on developing ways of increasing vagal tone in people who struggle with inflammatory conditions. He recognized that many factors can interfere with the ability of the vagus nerve to regulate the immune system.

article continues after advertisement

Over 20 years ago, implanted vagus nerve stimulators were approved by the FDA for the treatment of epilepsy, and later for severe depression. More recently, external stimulators have become available to the general public for use by applying the device to the neck or the ear several times a day to improve vagal tone. And Tracey has now developed a vagus nerve stimulator no bigger than a pill capsule, which can be surgically clipped onto one of the smaller branches of the vagus nerve for regulating one of the reflex arcs. Other ways to improve vagal tone include restful sleep, the daily practice of meditation, deep breathing, and some forms of exercise—all of which are useful, but may be hard to sustain as habits, and they don’t focus their effects on one organ.

Fortunately, revolutions in medicine roll in with the speed of molasses. This bioelectronic one does not yet have the power of large-scale global clinical trials with game-changing effects. Most clinicians will greet new studies in this area with caution until the number and quality of studies build a volume of evidence we can’t ignore.

Why should health psychologists, other therapists, and all of us future patients prepare for and welcome this “bioelectronic revolution?” As the science develops and the options increase for this alternative way to manage common chronic conditions, the transition process will place new demands and stressors on patients and clinicians. We are all going to have to change how we behave and think about illness. Therapy will guide these transitions in how we manage illness through major changes in skills, talk, thoughts, and behaviors.

Moving from attending to pillboxes and pharmacy refills to attending to stimulator apps and software settings will bring with it the turmoil that comes with any revolution. We can expect the pharmaceutical industry to oppose this bioelectronic revolution both overtly and covertly, since their share of the medical marketplace will shrink. Who knows how long the transition will take and how far it will go? Reading Tracey’s book The Great Nerve is one way to get ready.

item.title: On Becoming a Connoisseur of Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

On Becoming a Connoisseur of Anxiety

Learning to listen to, taste, savor, and learn from your anxiety.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is an inescapable and existential part of the human condition.
  • Rather than avoiding anxiety we must learn to tolerate, savor, and learn from it.
  • Creativity and productivity can come from liberating the energy of anxiety.

This is Part 3 of a series on anxiety. See Part 2 here.

Source: bricolage/Shutterstock

In much the same way that someone can become a connoisseur of fine wines, foods, or art, we not only can but, practically speaking, must all learn to become connoisseurs of anxiety. Anxiety is an inextricable thread running through the fabric of human existence. According to philosopher Søren Kierkegaard (1813-1855), anxiety (Angst) can be our 'best teacher," further asserting that "Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the ultimate." What does learning to be anxious "in the right way" really look like? A century later, existential psychotherapist Rollo May reminded us that, "In running from anxiety, you lose your most precious opportunities for the emergence of yourself." What did these astute students and distinguished connoisseurs of human anxiety mean by such enigmatic comments?

I call Kierkegaard and May connoisseurs of anxiety because they, like each of us to some extent, struggled with anxiety all their lives. Kierkegaard was brought up in a strictly religious household in Denmark, resulting in profound feelings of Christian guilt and anxiety. He encountered death and death anxiety after losing both of his parents and five of six siblings prior to turning 25 and, soon after, the profound pain and anxiety of lost romantic love following a self-sabotaged broken engagement. Later, Kierkegaard studied theology and was ordained as a Lutheran minister before deciding to become a philosopher instead, authoring his books Fear and Trembling (1843) and The Concept of Anxiety (1844) exploring the phenomenon and experience of anxiety, dread, or Angst.

Rollo May's early life took a somewhat similar trajectory to that of Kierkegaard, having been raised in a devoutly religious environment and eventually attending Union Theological Seminary, becoming an ordained minister. Unlike Kierkegaard, however, May served briefly as a pastor at a Congregational church in New Jersey before deciding to leave the ministry and become a clinical psychologist. His own childhood was deeply insecure, unstable, lonely, confusing, and anxiety-provoking, being the second eldest of six children, one of whom, his sister, suffered from schizophrenia. His parents eventually divorced, placing Rollo in the difficult position of becoming the caretaker for the family and his psychotic sister. Later, during his early 20s, while teaching English in Saloniki, Greece after graduating from college, May experienced what he himself diagnoses (1985) in hindsight as a "nervous breakdown." (See Diamond, 1986.)

At mid-life, May was stricken with tuberculosis, at that time a still frequently fatal disease, spending 18 months in a sanitorium fighting for his life and discovering the writings of Kierkegaard among others. It was then, during this enduring health crisis in which he was confronted with his own mortality, that he first conceived of the work that would become his doctoral dissertation and eventually his book The Meaning of Anxiety (1950). Despite his triumphant survival and success, May was subsequently dogged by anxiety and a sense of insecurity, neediness, and melancholy for most of his life, as documented in historian Robert Abzug's revealing recent biography. (See my prior post.) However, this predisposition toward anxiety did not prevent May from becoming one of the most prominent and renowned psychologists, public intellectuals, and bestselling psychological authors of the twentieth century. In fact, it motivated much of his professional and personal life, for better or worse.

article continues after advertisement

Stop, Listen, Feel, Savor, Learn

None of us is immune to experiencing anxiety, though its specific sources, symptoms, and triggers may differ greatly based on our genetics and particular life histories. The subjective and objective manifestations of anxiety can be complex and nuanced. But the ultimate origins of our anxiety are archetypal, universal, or existential: the intrinsic insecurity of existence, its seeming meaninglessness and absurdity, our own sense of insignificance and aloneness in an inconceivably immense and mysterious cosmos, and the ever-present existential realities of loss, suffering, evil, and death. Most of us try our best to avoid and hide our anxiety from others whenever possible, until that becomes no longer possible, at which time we are forced to confront and come to terms with it.

The key question when it comes to coping constructively with one's anxiety is really whether we are willing to stop worrying about and avoiding our feelings of anxiety long enough to carefully consider what it conceivably has to tell us. To courageously sink more fully into tasting and experiencing our anxiety rather than reflexively running from and rejecting it. To be more mindful of and present to it. (See my prior post.) Like its "kissing cousin" depression (see this fellow PT blogger's recent post), anxiety serves some function and purpose. Is it a warning of some kind? An alarm or wake-up call? Could it be symptomatic of an overactive thyroid or perhaps a sign of some other latent or intensifying physiological disease? A neurological artifact of some psychoactive stimulant, like caffeine, nicotine, cocaine, or methamphetamine? Or might it be a sign or "signal," i.e., signal anxiety, as Freud (1926) suggested, that we are resisting becoming more conscious of something unconscious within us? Or, might it possibly be some psychological call to arms, telling us it is time to make some major or minor necessary change in our lives? Perhaps to live more closely in alignment with our true self, psychological type, temperament, or sexual preference? Establish better balance in our personality or lifestyle? Seek some renewed sense of spiritual purpose and meaning? Pursue a more fulfilling work, social, or love life? Discover new ways to restore and sustain one’s soul, self, and sanity. Could your anxiety be a painful impetus to engage in some artistic or creative self-expression in the world? (I discuss the close ties between anger, anxiety, and creativity in my book Anger, Madness, and the Daimonic.) Or, might your anxiety be indicative of some existential anxiety, e.g., death anxiety or the anxiety that inevitably accompanies freedom, meaninglessness, and responsibility? Myriad meanings and purposes are possible.

Liberating and Expressing the Primal Energy of Anxiety

Anxiety, if we are willing to courageously follow wherever it leads, can serve as our own Ariadnean thread leading us, like the ancient Greek hero Theseus, out of the labyrinthine darkness of the unconscious and into the light of consciousness, illuminating the elusive message it may contain. Psychotherapy is one way of doing this. Creativity is another. Like anger and other daimonic emotions (see Diamond, 1996), anxiety is, fundamentally, a form of energy which, as the laws of physics hold, cannot be destroyed nor, as the laws of depth psychology suggest, indefinitely repressed, without a cost. The cost is that one's repressed or suppressed anxiety is negatively transmuted into various psychological and/or somatic symptoms. But when we choose to work instead toward reversing this alchemical process, refining and redirecting the raw, primal energy of our repressed anxiety into productive, creative, and constructive activity, this primal energy or vital life force is liberated. "During this process, we come to discover the paradox that many artists perceive: That which we had previously run from and rejected turns out to be the redemptive source of vitality, creativity, and authentic spirituality." (Diamond, 1991).

item.title: Is AI Making Work Better, or Just Making More Work?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is AI Making Work Better, or Just Making More Work?

The real promise of AI may be in helping us do less, not more.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Early research suggests that AI can intensify workloads, leading employees to work faster and longer.
  • AI can contribute to information overload by making it easier to produce content that others must process.
  • Research suggests that productivity drops sharply after 50 hours of work per week.
  • Organizations can use AI-driven efficiency gains to reduce workloads rather than simply assign more tasks.
Source: Hitesh Choudhary / Unsplash

An influential man at the top of his field—we’ll call him John for now—has predicted that advances in technology will usher in a revolution defined by dramatic gains in productivity. John is so optimistic about these gains that he suggests his grandchildren’s generation will likely need to work only about 15 hours a week. He shares that the real challenge for this future generation will not be how to manage work, but rather what to do with all their newfound free time.

John might sound like an AI optimist, echoing what many have hoped: that advances in artificial intelligence would make people’s lives better and help curb the burnout crisis facing so many workers. Yet John’s comments came well before AI, or even modern computers, existed. John, better known as the influential economist John Maynard Keynes, made these predictions in the 1930s.

Just as the technological advances of the nearly 100 years since Keynes made his prediction have not reduced working hours to anything close to what he envisioned (American workers average 42.9 hours per week), a similarly troubling pattern is emerging with AI: rather than translating productivity gains into less work, technological advances too often lead us to do more work instead. For example, initial research has shown that the increased output that comes with leveraging AI does not necessarily reduce our workload. Instead, it can intensify it. One study of 200 employees found that those leveraging generative AI consistently worked faster, took on a wider variety of tasks, and worked longer hours.

As we are still in the midst of the AI revolution, it is difficult to predict what AI will ultimately mean for our working hours and productivity. But one thing is worth considering: Just because technology makes it possible to do more doesn't mean we should. If we want AI to genuinely improve our working lives, we need to pause to consider if AI is making things better or worse. Two considerations are particularly important.

1. More Information Isn’t Always Better

Researchers Miriam Arnold and colleagues shared in 2023 that “the amount of information that is created every two days is roughly equivalent to the amount of information that was created between the beginning of human civilization and the year 2003.” With ChatGPT launching publicly in late 2022, this figure may have become even more extreme today.

With new information being created at such a staggering rate (and likely an accelerating one, given how AI has streamlined content creation), people have access to an almost unfathomable amount of information. However, having access to all this information does not mean we can actually absorb it.

Consider a study that examined how much information a new doctor in a narrow medical subspecialty (diagnostic imaging in cardiology) would need to read to get up to date. Assuming this doctor could dedicate all their time to reading, it would take approximately 11.34 years to catch up on the existing research. Yet even after all those years, they would still be behind. During that time, at least 80,000 additional papers would have been published, requiring another eight years of full-time reading just to catch up.

article continues after advertisement

This is an example of what many call information overload: the point at which the volume of available information becomes a burden, holding us back rather than pushing us forward. AI may help us manage some of this overload by making it easier to synthesize and prioritize information. But it can also exacerbate the problem by making it easier than ever to produce more content for others to sort through.

As AI makes it easier than ever to produce more, we need to be thoughtful about whether more is actually better. While AI might make us feel like we're getting more done, that additional output can create more work for those around us, especially when it becomes workslop (work that appears passable on the surface but lacks the substance needed to actually move things forward). Rather than simply asking how AI can help us do more, we should be asking whether what we're producing actually creates value. Sometimes, the most productive thing we can do is produce less.

2. More Time at Work Isn’t Always Better

In modern society, busyness has become a status symbol. In one study, participants who saw social media posts suggesting that someone was busy (such as “Oh, I have been working non-stop all week!” and “Quick 10-minute lunch”) assumed that these individuals had higher social status, higher socioeconomic status, and were more respected than those who posted about having free time (such as “I haven’t worked much this week, had lots of free time!” and “Enjoying a long lunch break”).

Busyness is similarly celebrated in the workplace. Many organizations have embraced what researchers call the ideal worker stereotype: someone who is always available and whose commitment to work is not limited by responsibilities outside of it.

Many half-glass-full-leaders had hoped that AI would reduce the amount of time people spend on routine tasks, freeing them up to work less. However, emerging research suggests that rather than simply reducing workloads, AI may be transforming them. As employees spend less time on tasks they previously performed, new AI-related responsibilities emerge to take their place.

article continues after advertisement

It is worth pausing to consider if we are headed in the right direction, given what we know about the relationship between working hours and productivity. While employees may feel pressure to work long hours to live up to the ideal worker stereotype, research suggests that productivity drops sharply after approximately 50 hours of work per week. The decline becomes so steep that someone working 55 hours is likely to produce roughly the same output as someone working 70.

If AI allows employees to complete a task in two hours instead of four, they face a choice. They can fill those two hours with additional responsibilities, or their leaders can allow them to benefit, at least in part, from the time saved. The latter might seem counterintuitive in a culture that celebrates busyness, but given what we know about the diminishing returns of long working hours, it may be the more productive choice. Rather than using the time AI saves us to simply take on more work, we should consider whether those hours might be better spent elsewhere. Sometimes, the most productive thing we can do is work less.

Nearly a century after Keynes imagined a future in which technology would give us more free time, AI is offering us a similar promise. Keynes's 15-hour workweek never became the norm, but perhaps this century can be different. The real opportunity may not be in how much more AI allows us to do, but in how much less we actually need to do.

item.title: Do Me a Favor!
item.description:
Altruism

Do Me a Favor!

Consider the subtle art of not asking for too much.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • The ultimatum game captures a simple but essential dynamics of negotiation.
  • In the favor-asking game, the petitioned party must pay so that the petitioner can gain.
  • The game yields high uncertainty and emotional risks.

I don’t like to be finessed. – Vartan Gregorian

The ultimatum game has achieved notoriety in behavioral economics and the study of negotiation. It’s a two-stage game. In stage 1, a proposer suggests how an available pot of money, say $10, be shared with a receiver. The receiver then has a choice between accepting the deal and rejecting it; if the latter, no one gets anything. Conventional game theory says the proposer should offer the smallest amount possible, that is, $1 if only single-dollar bills are on the table. The receiver should accept this offer because having any money should be preferred to having none (Güth et al., 1982).

If the reader’s intuition rebels, this is as it should be. Fairness matters. Receivers can punish selfish proposers, and when they do, their loss is smaller than the proposers’ loss. Righteous retribution can feel good (Jackson et al., 2019). The veto-saying receiver teaches the greedy proposer a lesson, and this is not nothing in the hedonic calculus. Proposers are, however, as smart as receivers, and so they can anticipate that very small offers will be rejected (Thielmann & Hilbig, 2014). They therefore tend to offer the smallest amount that they themselves would accept if they were in the receiver’s role. This shakes out to be about $3 to $4.

The ultimatum game is a game where one player seeks to force the other player’s hand. Proposers move in such a way that the receiver’s best response is favorable to the proposer. Now consider a variant of the ultimatum game, an exchange in the domain of favor-asking. Suppose the first mover has entered a situation where much is at stake. They can either gain a large amount of money, say $1,000, or lose that same amount, leaving them in debt. What happens now depends on what the second mover does. Mover 1 says to mover 2, please pay a small fine of $10 so that I can realize my large gain; if you don’t pay that small fine, I will be in debt by $1,000. Both players possess credible information that mover 1 cannot share any eventual gains with mover 2 by way of a bribe after the fact. There is a vigilant enforcer on duty who will ensure that the rules of the game will not be finessed.

In this game, mover 1 faces the stress of having to figure out if mover 2 can be trusted. Will mover 2 be kind enough to shoulder the fee, or will mover 2 at least be moved by guilt to pay up, even if there is resentment to be swallowed? Mover 2, in turn, needs to figure out if there is enough of generosity, kindness, or altruism within them to make a larger gain to mover 2 outweigh the small cost to the self. An atheoretical approach to empirical exploration would consider all possible pairings of gains, losses, and fines to estimate the relative utilities of the self’s gains and losses and the other’s gains and losses. Where the lines intersect, that’s where the equilibrium must lie.

The psychology implicated in this game is a bit thicker. Mover 2 may literally feel being played when informed that the fate of mover 1 now lies in their hands. While some players may see no problem, others will balk at having their hand forced (Brehm & Cole, 1966). Much like the receiver in the conventional ultimatum game, they can punish a presumptuous proposer.

article continues after advertisement

A common variant of this game is when a person is in distress, and critically so, thanks in part to their own failure to be prudent. They now turn to another person to bail them out. They will likely look to approach someone they think ‘can’t say no’ because of pre-existing emotional bonds, shared interests, or other forms of mutual indebtedness. The sought help may be given, but at the risk of relational damage and admonitions to ‘not do this again!’ Note that this game is different from a bystander scenario, where one person is in distress and another (a stranger) is available to avert the worst outcome at a small cost to themselves (Fischer et al., 2011). The bystander situation is a volunteer’s dilemma played out among potential helpers (Krueger, 2019). The favor-asking game, in contrast, is a form of risky negotiation.

Under some circumstances the stress and the distress of the favor game can be avoided. This de-escalation can be achieved by simple pre-game communication. A first mover who informs the second mover about their intention to play and who requests a self-prediction or commitment from the second mover up front might do well. This, however, is a big ‘might.’ A second mover who is given a choice before the fact has an out. They can tell the first mover: ‘I will not help you, so do not get yourself into trouble.’ The favor-asking game is intriguing because the uninformed second mover may now, in fact, be more willing to help because of the fait which was accomplit by the first mover. Alternatively, if they are not guilt prone and if they are averse to being finessed, second movers might balk. Taken together, this should mean that those who spring requests for favors onto others have to resign themselves to knowing that they will learn from experience.

Illustrative real-world scenarios come to mind, and the tension they involve is palpable. One occasionally observed theme, and which is popular in TV dramas, features generational conflict. The young have overspent, gone into debt, or had their naivité exploited by ruthless others. They turn to elder relatives (e.g., parents) as the help of last resort (Andersen et al., 2020). Will the elders help – and if so, should they worry about long-term downsides (Krueger, 2026)?
